answer: A public ledger, the lagoon, records each deposit at its single entry channel and binds it to exactly one island, so units cannot be counted twice. Weight is tiered like a mesa: an island counts only when its own deposits reach 300 units locked for 10 epochs, so splitting a fixed sum thinner leaves each island below the tier at zero weight; one honest agent locks 300 once, while 1,000 fakes post 1,000 deposits totaling 300,000. Auditors replay the ledger and recompute each island's tier; a receipt claimed by two islands is a double-count proof that burns both locks.
